mill-pond-inn.name: Mill Pond Inn
sign: Pizza night Wednesdays, chalked by the door in a hand that has written it a hundred times.
The mill pond sits right behind the place, and on a warm evening the door stays propped so the talk carries out over the water.

jefferson-town-hall.name: Jefferson Town Hall
sign: Posted hours end at 2 PM most days. The board agenda lists road salt bids and 'the goat situation (continued).'
Meeting nights are posted, court sits about once a month, and metal recycling is the first Saturday. Small things, kept up carefully.

heartbreak-hotel.name: Heartbreak Hotel
sign: A hand-lettered sign by the door: PRIME RIB SATURDAY. MAKE A RESERVATION. WE MEAN IT.
Two hearts up under the roofline, a porch light on early, and somebody inside already laughing at the bar.

middle-brook-cafe.name: Middle Brook Cafe
sign: The stone patio out front is filling up, and there is a cup on nearly every table catching the morning sun.
Inside, a customer is explaining, with great intensity, that the chocolate chip cookie is somehow vegan.

stewarts.name: Stewart's
sign: Coffee in one hand and a cone in the other, and the whole junction of NY 10 and NY 23 going by the window.
Taped to the ice cream case inside, a hand-written sheet keeps the softball league standings current.

mac-a-doodles.name: Mac-A-Doodles
sign: Ice cream is the main event here: the soft-serve window, cones going out steadily, and kids at the counter choosing with real seriousness.
A dog outside is finishing a pup cup with real focus. The menu board also offers a mac-n-cheese burger, and it is not a dare.

stamford-coffee.name: Stamford Coffee
sign: The patio out front is half the building: tables full, a dog asleep under one, and somebody ordering a Maple Smoke latte.
Inside, the pastry case is lit up beside the register and every table has somebody's afternoon on it.
This is where the week gets talked over. Through the side doorway, 80 Main's shelves are calling.

the-belvedere.name: The Belvedere
sign: Up the hill and lit early, and it sounds like everybody in there knows everybody.
It was a hotel once, and it is still that big. These days the bar is the part that's open, and the bar is plenty.
Inside: one long bar with stools down three sides of it, foosball, a little corner stage, and a wall of chalk behind the taps.
A taped-up flyer teases a big-name comedian, headed this way one of these days. DATE TBA. Guess you'll just have to keep checking back.

cellar-door-wines.name: Cellar Door Wines
sign: Through the window, the owner is walking a couple through an Austrian orange wine. Nobody leaves this shop empty-handed.
Out front there is a bench, and if you sit on it for any length of time a friend is sure to stop in.

tops.name: Tops
sign: Carts nosed into the corral, the bulletin board by the door three layers deep, and half the lot waving at the other half.
Someone loading a trunk, to nobody in particular: "Produce selection isn't great, but it beats a thirty-minute trip when you forgot the milk."

stamford-library.name: Stamford Library
sign: A jigsaw half-done on the table inside the window, one whole corner still sky. A card beside it: TAKE A PIECE, LEAVE A PIECE.
Story hour Thursday mornings, says the sign on the door, in careful marker with a cat drawn in the corner.

stamford-fire-department.name: Stamford Fire Department
sign: Chalked on a board by the bay doors: PANCAKE BREAKFAST SUNDAY, 8 TO NOON. Underneath, smaller: chicken barbecue in July.
Half the town volunteers here, on their own time, and the other half turns up for the pancakes. Every name on the roster inside is somebody you passed on Main Street today.

solinskys.name: Solinsky's
sign: The smoke reaches the sidewalk a few doors early, and there is already a friendly little line of regulars working its way to the case.
Sign by the register: BRISKET SANDWICHES SATURDAY. Underneath, in a different hand: come early, they go.

johns-tavern.name: John's Tavern
sign: Door propped open, a game on somewhere in the back, and a laugh going up at something that happened three innings ago.
Nobody dresses up for John's, and nobody needs to. Grab a stool; somebody will want to know how your week went.

eighty-main.name: 80 Main
sign: Candles and mugs made close to home on one shelf, and on the next a very good sweater and some camo that is more fashion than deer season.
Its door and Stamford Coffee's open onto the same patio, so a browse and a cup of coffee turn into one errand.

tps-cafe.name: T.P.'s Cafe
sign: Breakfast comes right out onto Railroad Avenue: eggs, toast, coffee going round. Half the stools at the counter know each other's orders.
Ace Hardware is right next door, so breakfast here tends to come with a plan for the afternoon.

ace-hardware.name: Ace Hardware
sign: Saturday morning, and the lot is full: a good share of it people who moved up here, bought a place that needed work, and are happily still at it.
Someone comes in holding one mystery part; someone behind the counter says "aisle four, halfway down" without looking up.

jh-gas-station.name: J&H
sign: Pumps out front, and a deli counter inside that has most of the village's mornings covered: coffee, egg sandwiches, and the first news of the day.
Half the trucks in the lot belong to somebody's contractor. If you have been trying to reach one, this is where they all are at seven in the morning.

lines: NY 10 keeps going north out of Jefferson, on up the valley. Another week, maybe.
Creamery Street runs on south, out past where the old creameries once stood. Another day's walk.
Main Street carries on west out of the village. Another week, maybe.
Harper Street keeps going west out of the village, NY 23 the whole way. Another week, maybe.
Main Street runs on east as NY 23, out along the valley. Another week, maybe.
The old rail bed keeps running this way too — the Catskill Scenic Trail covers a lot of ground. Another day's walk.
You keep going past the last of the houses, and the trees close in behind you, and after a while every direction starts to look like the same direction.
You call the Delaware County Sheriff's Office. The dispatcher couldn't be kinder: happens to the best of us, those woods go on for miles, stay right where you are.
The deputy waits until you're steady on your feet, then nods toward the door.
"Get yourself a coffee," they say. "And maybe stick to the sidewalks for a while."
A chalkboard by the door, wiped and rewritten so many times it has gone soft and grey.
TONIGHT: tacos, then a movie. Underneath, smaller: whoever turns up, whatever they feel like.
NY 10 keeps going as Main Street runs out, south toward Delhi. Another week, maybe.
Maple Avenue keeps going south past the bridge. Another day's walk.

people.name: Hannah
lines: Morning! Coffee's on — it has been since half past four, and it'll still be on whenever you wander back in.
The ice cream case is right over there, and yes, the make-your-own sundae bar is real. Nobody has ever been sorry about a sundae.
Somebody asked me once if our coffee costs more than Dunkin. It's cheaper, actually — and the nearest Dunkin is a good long drive from here. This one's right here.
A single bathroom, and a good one: clean, a plant on the cistern, and a hand-lettered sign asking you kindly to jiggle the handle.
Anyone can use it. There is a hook for your coat, and the soap smells like lemons.
The other one, just the same, with a changing table folded against the wall and a stack of the good paper towels.
Whichever is free is yours.
A whole shelf of coffee makers, every kind there is: a glass pour-over, a stovetop moka pot, a siphon like something out of a science set, a percolator with a few decades on it.
They all still work, and most of them get used. It is a collection, not a museum.
The menu, in chalk: coffee every way you could want it, the Maple Smoke latte in a box of its own, and a row of paninis pressed to order — the kind you smell before you see.
Nothing on this board you would regret.

Bottles behind the right end of the counter: a cooler of beer from breweries an easy drive from here, and a few bottles of wine to take home, each with a little card in Ronnie's hand saying what it goes with.
Ask at the counter and one goes home with you. One of these evenings, one will.
A record player on the left wall, lid up, something warm and a little crackly turning on it.
Whoever is behind the counter picks the side. It is always the right one.
Crates of LPs, spread out so you can flip through them: jazz, old country, soul, and a few things nobody can quite place.
Every sleeve has been handled a hundred times, which is exactly what they are for.
The furniture is mid-century modern, all of it: low tables, tapered legs, chairs that look like they came off a magazine cover in 1958 and have been sat in happily ever since.
Nothing matches exactly, and it all goes together anyway.
A self-serve fridge up by the door: cold drinks, snacks, and ready-made dinners for anyone who would rather not cook tonight.
Help yourself, says the little sign on it. One of these weeks, you might.

people.name: Ronnie
lines: Morning. The board's right here — the Maple Smoke latte's the one everybody asks about. And if there are lemon shortbreads left in the case, grab one now; we can't keep them in stock.
That's my record on. Have a flip through the crates by the player if you like — there's always something good in there.
Take your time picking a table. The big doorway on the right goes straight through to 80 Main, and the bathrooms are up the hallway in the corner on the left — the steel door off it is the kitchen.
The oven, two big decks of it, ticking as it warms. Most mornings it's scones and muffins for the case out front, and the whole kitchen smells of them.
There's a timer on a string hung on the hook beside it. Somebody's never once needed it.
Steel work tables all along the wall: the big stand mixer, a scale that weighs to the gram, and a bench scraper worn smooth from years of good use.
This is where the coffee shop's own baking gets done — the scones, the cookies, whatever goes in the case each morning.
Two fridges and a chest freezer, humming in three different keys: butter by the case, eggs by the flat, milk and cream for the espresso machine out front.
Everything in here is going to be breakfast for somebody by the end of the week.
A table kept clear at the end of the room, with a turntable and a rack of food colours on the shelf above it.
Some nights a baker borrows the kitchen after the shop's locked up and builds her custom cakes here. Most days it's just where the trays get stacked.
A rolling rack of trays, cooling: lemon shortbread cookies, every tray of them. They go out front by the dozen and they're gone.
Buttery, a little sharp, sugar on top. One is never the number.
Catskills-logo wear, a whole wall of it: hats, tees, hoodies, the mountains stitched small over the heart.
You would wear it home, and then keep wearing it.
A very good sweater, folded the way only a shop folds things, and beside it some camo that is more fashion than deer season.
Both would look right on Main Street. Both would look right anywhere.
Candles and mugs made close to home, the kind you pick up to look at properly and then keep holding.
Everything on this shelf was chosen by somebody who liked it first.
A low table of wool throws and blankets, folded in the colours the hills go in October.
Somebody has already run a hand over every one of them today. You do too.
More of the logo wear, out where you can get at it: beanies in a basket, a stack of tees, hoodies on a rail with the mountains over the heart.
The good stuff is the stuff you will still be wearing in ten years, and this is the good stuff.
A coffee table made of coal. Polished, black, heavier than it looks, and yes — really coal.
They have sold one, and they may still. Somebody, somewhere, sets a cup down on it every morning.
OYSTER & WINE NIGHT, the board says: some evenings the shop stays open late, the oysters come out on ice and the wine comes out with them.
Ask at the counter which night. It is worth planning a week around.

people.name: Tamsin
lines: Come on in and have a look round. Everything here is the kind of thing we would want ourselves.
The sweaters run true to size, and the mugs are from just up the road.
The coffee shop is right through the doorway on the left. The two of us have always been one visit.
The whole wall behind the bar is a blackboard, and somebody is always partway through covering it.
This month it's a chalk mural of the valley, road and river and all, drawn by whoever got the ladder first.
They papered over this whole wall, and it looks like there are glass doors behind it.
Behind those, they say, is the old hotel's swimming pool — dry for years, and still there.
Somebody drew on this wall once, and everybody has been adding to it ever since.
Every hand in town is on it: a dog, a mountain, a pickup, a heart with two names in it, one very good cow, and plenty of penises.
A note taped to this bathroom door, in marker: CLOSED UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE. It has been there a while, and it is not going anywhere.
Underneath, in a different pen: it's alright, the other bathroom's nicer anyway.
The other bathroom: a urinal, a stall, and no sign on the door saying who it's for.
There's a latch on the inside if you'd like the room to yourself.

people.name: Marnie
lines: Evening. Grab any stool you like.
Anything you need, I'm right here. I'm always right here.

See that papered-over wall? Old hotel pool back there, dry for years. The mayor — he sells real estate too — walked new owners out onto the plywood over it once and went clean through. Dry as a bone under there, thank goodness.
You take a split log off the pile. Dry, and lighter than it looks.
otherwise: You've already got one under your arm. One at a time is how the fire likes it.
fixtures.heldBlurb: A split log off the Belvedere's pile, tucked under your arm for the fire.

lines: You set the log on the fire and it catches.
Everybody round the ring leans back an inch, and somebody says thanks without looking up.
otherwise: The fire's going fine; it could use a log from the pile.
